set.note: Usually negative. Do not confuse with saccharin (no final e), the artificial sweetener.

why: Note claims the adjective comes from saccharin; false: the adjective dates from the 1670s, the sweetener was named in 1879 (etymonline)
winsome (sweet, charming) overlaps the 'sweet' part of the def for question (b)
weary means tired, not lacking energy and interest
'uninhibited designs broke every rule' also fits the cloze sensibly
calm and gentle are not synonyms of 'wanting to avoid fighting'
tough is not a synonym of thin-but-muscular
spring (from) means to originate, not to come out of a source like light or smell

set.def: of police or officials: to take away and hold property, such as a car, until a fine is paid or a matter is settled

why: 'until a rule is met' is unclear and inaccurate
peal and chime are cheerful or musical ringing, not a slow funeral bell
drudgery (boring repetitive work) is a near-synonym; fits (b), (e) and the cloze
'the senator slyly avoided answering' also fits the cloze
limitless/limited are loose, not true synonym/antonym in this sense
wrecker is rare and subversive means someone who undermines a government, not a true synonym
'liberal' as opposite is ambiguous and politically loaded
irk (annoy, keeps bothering) overlaps the also-sense 'worry or trouble someone steadily' for question (g)
pester (annoy) is a near-synonym of rile; fits (b) and (e)
overhear means hearing by accident, the opposite of secret deliberate listening
